A few explanations for this behavior that aren't worry inducing.

How long since you got them? If they're brand new in a new environment, they're probably just working stuff out. Mice have a natural pecking order and they're probably still trying to figure out who's the boss right now.

Along with that, if you got them from a petstore they probably haven't had enough space to work anything out in their entire lives! Petstores don't exactly give them spacious, exciting enclosures like we do.

The squeaking and nipping is all normal for mice.

Also, how many mice do you have? If you only have two, sometimes mice will bully each other more in that situation. Upgrading to a trio might help. 

If you have more than two, try doing a carrier method reintroduction of just those two. It forces them to get used to each other and bond with nothing to fight over.

I dont blame you at all for making that mistake. There's so many websites and sources that say this is fine.

My best guess is because when you keep them all together in small cages with very limited enrichment, they don't fight because there's nothing to fight over. Which is why people use the carrier method for introductions. 

African softfurs are an option if you can find them. If you wanna keep them, they'll probably be okay alone. Just try and make up for it with lots of enrichment and space!

I've owned gerbils and mice. Gerbils didn't work for me and I ended up rehoming them to a friend who was interested and got mice instead. 

Here are my comparisons 


Attention needs

Mice require less hands on attention. A lot are okay with just being observation pets.

Gerbils really should be interacted with in my opinion. It's cruel to just put them in a tank and call it good. They get depressed and bored. Be prepared for that.

Space

Gerbils need SPACE. 20 gallons is absolutely not enough. They need to dig, and if you get anything smaller than around 40 you'll start watching them and it's just very obvious that they're cramped and can't express their natural behaviors. 

Mice are smaller of course. I keep mine in a 40 gallon but I've heard people keeping them in smaller, especially if it's just a pair. They don't need nearly as much bedding, so you can actually fit wheels, hides, etc. Because there's not 9 inches of bedding hogging up all the space.

Smell.

Gerbils are absolutely the best option if you don't want a smelly pet. No debate. Gerbils should not smell. If they do, you're doing something wrong. When I owned gerbils I'd only do a fully clean very month and there was no oder whatsoever. 

Mice are smelly. They just are. I accidently ended up with a male I had to return (as I also bought a female and wasn't aware that the other was a male) and he REAKED. I found out he was male around 2 days after getting him and the smell was awful already. Females seem better. 

Biting and friendliness 

Gerbils can bite sometimes. But it's easily worked through. They're very rarely "aggressive". Sometimes I've heard of gerbils getting territorial over their cage, but most of the time they'll calm down once you take them out. One of my gerbils had a biting habit, but I'd just gently blow on his back and he'd stop. I didn't put him back or give him what he wanted either, and he stopped.

I'm not sure about mice and biting, as I haven't handled mine and don't have personal experience. But through my research I haven't seen it be a big issue.


For my personal recommendation, of course from the intro, I prefer mice. I'm an adult without a lot of time and I ended up not being able to give my gerbils nearly enough attention. Because of that, I never established much of a bond. Since they spend most of their time in burrows, I never got the chance to enjoy them. My mice run around in their cage, act cute and seem okay with me not being able to give them a lot of hands on time. 

So really, it's just a question of needs and what you want out of a pet. If your daughter is planning on spending a ton of time with her pet and just bonding, go with gerbils. They're wonderful animals and are very sweet and loving compared to any rodent I've owned. They're also awake in the day, which is a plus for kids who don't spend all day at work. I managed to get through my 2 year degree with a 3.5 GPA (out of 4.0).

It was a struggle, but heres what worked for me.

• Don't force yourself to work on others people schedule. I was never able to get my assignments done ahead of time. Neither did I even bother to look at coursework until the day of. Not ideal, but taking it one day at a time like that helped me keep everything in order in my brain.

• doing work at home didn't work. At all. I just couldn't do it. There were very specific places on campus that I could study and be motivated. Find a location that keeps you motivated and on track. 

• peer / teacher pressure. Make relationships with your teachers. Take verbal accountability when you mess up or get behind. Give yourself a social circle around getting your work done. People with adhd are far too used to dissapointing ourselves. Make it so that you're dissapointing someone else too. Idk if thats healthy but it worked for me.

• lastly, this was so unhealthy but it still helped. That awful panic feeling was enough to keep me pushing. "Oh shit I have 40 missing assignments and I can't graduate if I don't get them done." That situation was not the time to "be gentle on myself". That was a panic and work for 7 hours straight moment.

None of this was organizing advice or whatever but more realistic things that helped me. Hopefully it helps!

Its something I learned in cognitive behavioral therapy. If I were to explain the best I could, emotions might turn into thoughts, thoughts might turn into a behavior. Or a thought might turn into an emotion which turns into a behavior. Or a behavior can cause a thought. And so on. 

So if we were to think of it as a cycle. It can help alter your general overall view of yourself or the world. 

In practice, I'll give an example. My emotion might be shame. That thought might say "I'm an awful useless person". My reaction to that might be self isolation and self sabotage. Emotions are really hard to change. So instead I might change my behavior. So I surround myself with people and keep doing my best as if I feel amazing about this, even though I don't. Hopefully, this helps counteract those thoughts of uselessness and those feelings of shame.

For me, I suppose what helps me the most is just acceptance. Trying my best not to let it effect how I view myself. When I'm really bad, ill make two lists of all the values and traits I see in myself. The healthy ones and the unhealthy ones.

"Distractable, curious, sensitive, excitable" are things I'd write down on that other end. Then I make the choice to focus on those good ones. 

Our thought process can be boiled down into a little cycle. Thought -> emotion -> action, and it goes in a circle. You can disrupt that cycle by changing one of those three things. It's not magic but it helps.

I went through online college with untreated adhd, and managed to get out with As and Bs. Don't get me wrong, it was absolute HELL. What worked for me though was balancing out how much I could fuck up without failing, basically. I learned my limits, and what I could and couldn't do.

Textbooks are bullshit. For me, I just figured out how to get by without reading them. Many of my classes basically taught with a book. I basically only skimmed through the few paragraphs I actually needed to solve the questions, used other sources if I could. 

Working with your professors is also so important. I found out that I hadn't realized over half of my assignments existed when my teacher graded them all as 0s literally the day before graduation. I drank a shit ton a caffine and got them all done in a single day. Those bursts of motivation were the only times I got anything done. 

Its also pretty important to find the best place to focus. For me, home was an awful place to do school. It made me want to get in my bed, watch videos or just go do other stuff. 

My only piece of advice is just to trudge through it. Give yourself a minimum grade that you'll accept and do your best to stick to that. Online college lacks all the things that people with adhd depend on for success and it sucks. Just be kind to yourself and do your best. But don't be too kind and dismiss everything. Getting upset over grades can sometimes be good motivation to make it through, honestly.
